title: Dandelion: Redesigning the Bitcoin Network for Anonymity
note: Introduces Dandelion: transactions first travel a randomly chosen path (stem, anonymity phase) and are then diffused (fluff). Adversary: passive, graph-aware coalition of spy nodes (fraction p of the network) that follow the protocol, timestamp first receipt, and want to link a transaction to the originating IP; gives near-optimal precision bounds among schemes without extra encryption.
bitmessage_link: Direct answer to flooding exposing the origin: Bitmessage floods an object to all peers at once so the first-hearing node is a strong source estimator; stem/fluff is the standard repair, and Bitmessage later added a Dandelion-style stem.

title: Dandelion++: Lightweight Cryptocurrency Networking with Formal Anonymity Guarantees
note: Dandelion++ replaces per-hop line-graph construction with a 4-regular privacy graph, per-epoch routing and fail-safe timers. Adversary: colluding fraction p of nodes that may deviate from the protocol (drop, inject, collude on duplicates), knows the graph and observes first-receipt times; formal near-optimal precision/recall guarantees with a lightweight local rule.
bitmessage_link: Reference design for hiding origin in a flooding network without encryption; the Bitmessage stem phase and most later P2P messengers that borrow it follow this construction.

title: BIP 156: Dandelion - Privacy Enhancing Routing
note: Wire-level specification of Dandelion (stem and fluff phases, embargo timers, fail-safe). Adversary model is inherited from Dandelion: spy nodes that observe relay timing; the BIP was closed without being merged into Bitcoin Core.
bitmessage_link: Shows what a deployed flooding network needs in order to add a stem phase (message type, embargo timer), a requirement Bitmessage-style object flooding would share.

title: DANDELION (Logos/Waku application specification)
note: Raw-status specification of a Dandelion-style stem/fluff layer for Waku relay messages. Adversary: passive observers among relay peers who attribute a message to the first peer to deliver it.
bitmessage_link: Applies Dandelion to a gossip publish/subscribe messenger, the closest modern analogue of Bitmessage-style flooding plus a source-hiding stem.

title: GOSSIPSUB-TOR-PUSH
note: Specification for pushing the first hop of a gossipsub message through Tor circuits so that subscribed peers cannot attribute the origin to the publisher IP. Adversary: gossipsub peers (and network observers of the publisher link) who learn origin from the first sender; assumes Tor as the anonymity transport.
bitmessage_link: Tor-based propagation of the first hop, the Tor analogue of Dandelion for gossip pub/sub; contrasts with Bitmessage, which connects directly or via Tor at user option.

title: Deanonymisation of clients in Bitcoin P2P network
note: Links transaction pseudonyms to client IPs using the set of entry (outgoing-connection) nodes as a fingerprint, also behind NAT. Adversary: well-connected passive observer running a few machines that connect to many reachable nodes and watches relay order; also an active step that abuses anti-DoS bans to cut off Tor use.
bitmessage_link: Shows that an observer connected to many peers de-anonymises the origin of flooded messages, the attack that motivated Dandelion and applies equally to Bitmessage objects.

title: Bitcoin over Tor isn't a good idea
note: Shows that routing Bitcoin through Tor lets a low-resource attacker control all Tor-using clients by getting them banned from exit nodes and steering them to attacker nodes, then link transactions. Adversary: active attacker with a few Tor exit relays and Bitcoin nodes, abusing Bitcoin DoS defences (ban scores) to force connections.
bitmessage_link: Cautionary result for using Tor as the transport of a flooding network: a peer-reputation or anti-DoS rule keyed on source address can be turned into a steering attack.

title: Spy vs. Spy: Rumor Source Obfuscation
note: Introduces adaptive diffusion: the virtual source moves away from the true source so that the infected set has an obfuscating shape. Adversary: global observer of a snapshot of the infected set (and optionally timestamps) with rumor-centrality style source estimators.
bitmessage_link: Defines the snapshot-adversary model for flooding and a spreading rule that hides the origin without cryptography; background for any analysis of who learns what from a flood.

title: Hiding the Rumor Source
note: Journal version of adaptive diffusion with perfect-obfuscation proof on regular trees under the snapshot adversary and bounds when timestamp metadata is sampled. Adversary: global snapshot adversary, optionally with sampled timestamps; shows a fundamental trade-off between spreading speed and obfuscation.
bitmessage_link: Gives provable limits on source hiding under flooding; shows source-hiding costs latency, consistent with Bitmessage choosing flood speed over origin privacy.

title: Anonymity Properties of the Bitcoin P2P Network
note: Models Bitcoin trickle and diffusion spreading and proves poor anonymity against a first-spy and maximum-likelihood adversary on regular trees, validated on a 2015 topology snapshot. Adversary: supernode connected to all nodes (eavesdropper) plus spy-node coalitions; changing from flooding to diffusion did not help.
bitmessage_link: Proves that randomised-delay diffusion does not hide the origin of a gossip flood against a well-connected observer; this is the formal basis for treating Bitmessage origin as exposed.

title: On the Anonymity of Peer-To-Peer Network Anonymity Schemes Used by Cryptocurrencies
note: Bayesian framework giving per-transaction originator distributions; evaluates Dandelion, Dandelion++ and Lightning Network onion routing. Adversary: colluding nodes (1 to 15 percent, strategically placed) observing messages; finds Lightning Network 1 percent colluders identify the originator of about 50 percent of payments, and Dandelion anonymity set does not grow with network size.
bitmessage_link: Quantifies how little Dandelion-style stems and onion-routed payment paths hide, so stem-phase source hiding in a Bitmessage-like system should not be read as strong anonymity.

title: Clover: an Anonymous Transaction Relay Protocol for the Bitcoin P2P Network
note: Clover relays a transaction through a randomly chosen proxy chain without building a propagation graph and limits the gain of an adversary opening many connections to one node. Adversary: eavesdropper observing the whole network (first-spy and rumor-centrality style) and a node-opening adversary; reports up to 10x lower deanonymisation accuracy than diffusion in simulation.
bitmessage_link: Simpler proxy-style alternative to Dandelion++ for hiding who first sent a flooded object.

title: Deanonymization and Linkability of Cryptocurrency Transactions Based on Network Analysis
note: Clusters transactions by relay-timing patterns and links clusters to IPs for Bitcoin and Zcash, and shows ADDR messages help attribution. Adversary: passive well-connected observer that logs relay timings and address advertisements; reports high precision and recall on own transactions in Bitcoin and Zcash.
bitmessage_link: Network-level deanonymisation of a flooded transaction in Bitcoin and Zcash; applies to any flooding messenger that exposes timing and address gossip.

title: Deanonymizing Bitcoin Transactions via Network Traffic Analysis with Semi-supervised Learning
note: NTSSL: transaction deanonymisation combining network traffic analysis with semi-supervised learning (pseudo-labels from unsupervised clustering) and NTSSL+ with cross-layer transaction clustering; reported 1.6x better than a prior ML approach. Adversary: passive network observer with traffic traces and few labels.
bitmessage_link: Machine-learning traffic analysis on top of flooding: shows source timing leakage persists under transport encryption.

title: ethp2psim: Evaluating and deploying privacy-enhanced peer-to-peer routing protocols for the Ethereum network
note: Simulator to evaluate and deploy privacy-enhanced P2P transaction routing protocols (Dandelion++-like, k-anonymous variants) for Ethereum against first-spy style adversaries. Adversary: passive network observers and spy coalitions placed at configurable positions.
bitmessage_link: Tooling for comparing source-hiding gossip variants; relevant when estimating how a flood-based messenger leaks origin.

title: Deanonymizing Ethereum Validators: The P2P Network Has a Privacy Issue
note: Any node can link a validator to the hosting peer by observing which attestations a peer forwards outside its subnet duties; finds over 15 percent of validators in 3 days with four nodes. Adversary: passive peer with ordinary connections in a gossipsub overlay with deterministic subscription duties.
bitmessage_link: Origin inference from subscription duty in a pub/sub overlay: subscription structure itself, not only timing, reveals who publishes.

title: Deanonymizing Monero Transactions in Tor Network
note: ProxyMark: a Monero node using Tor sends originated transactions only to two outgoing Tor hidden-service proxy nodes before clearnet spread, so an adversary occupying those outgoing connections sees origin. Adversary: active node that fills the victim outgoing slots on the Tor path; tested on live Tor, mainnet and testnet.
bitmessage_link: Anonymity-network transport plus Dandelion++ still leaks when peer selection is restricted; shows peer-selection hardening matters for source privacy.

title: Metadata-Conscious Anonymous Messaging
venue: IEEE Transactions on Signal and Information Processing over Networks 2016
note: Anonymous messaging over a social or peer graph that accounts for observer-visible metadata (spread shape and timing); extends adaptive diffusion. Adversary: global observer with snapshot and partial timestamp metadata.
bitmessage_link: Treats the flooding pattern itself as leaking metadata, the core weakness of Bitmessage-style broadcast.

title: Bandwidth-Efficient Transaction Relay for Bitcoin (Erlay)
note: Replaces most announcement flooding with set reconciliation, cutting announcement bandwidth by about 40 percent at the cost of some latency. Adversary: none (efficiency); notes that reconciliation changes which timing signals a spy can use, relevant to source-anonymity analyses.
bitmessage_link: Concrete bandwidth limit of announce-everything flooding and a reconciliation fix, the cost side of the Bitmessage download-everything design.

title: Anonymity Trilemma: Strong Anonymity, Low Bandwidth Overhead, Low Latency - Choose Two
note: Proves that strong sender or recipient anonymity against a global passive network adversary needs either high bandwidth overhead or high latency; gives constraints that grow with compromised nodes. Adversary: global passive network observer, optionally with a passively compromised subset of protocol nodes.
bitmessage_link: Formal reason a flood-to-everyone design pays bandwidth (every node downloads everything) to buy recipient anonymity at low latency.

title: On Privacy Notions in Anonymous Communication
note: Unified hierarchy of sender, recipient and relationship anonymity notions and adversary assumptions for anonymous communication networks. Adversary: parameterised (passive or active, corrupted users, global or local).
bitmessage_link: Vocabulary for stating exactly which of sender, recipient or relationship anonymity a flooding broadcast gives and against which observer.

title: On the Complexity of Anonymous Communication Through Public Networks
note: Lower bounds on communication needed for anonymous communication through public networks against an adversary that sees all traffic and compromises a fraction of nodes. Adversary: global passive observer plus corrupted nodes.
bitmessage_link: Lower bounds that contextualise the Bitmessage bandwidth cost of broadcast.

title: Eclipse Attacks on Bitcoin's Peer-to-Peer Network
note: Shows an adversary controlling many IPs can monopolise all of a victim node's incoming and outgoing connections by poisoning its address tables, and proposes countermeasures later merged in Bitcoin Core (deterministic bucketing, feeler connections, more table slots). Adversary: attacker with a botnet or a few ASes, control of many IP addresses in distinct groups, no need to be on-path.
bitmessage_link: An eclipsed Bitmessage node sees only attacker objects and attacker peers, so it can be denied messages or have its source anonymity and recipient scan targeted; peer-table hardening is the defence.

title: Low-Resource Eclipse Attacks on Ethereum's Peer-to-Peer Network
note: Eclipse attacks on Ethereum Geth nodes using two hosts, exploiting node ID generation, the discovery table and connection-slot rules; countermeasures merged in Geth. Adversary: attacker with a small number of IP addresses (one to two hosts) and the ability to generate arbitrary node IDs.
bitmessage_link: Kademlia-style discovery with free identities is cheap to eclipse; matters for any DHT-assisted peer finding for a flooding messenger.

title: Eclipsing Ethereum Peers with False Friends
note: False-friends eclipse on Geth by exploiting Kademlia-inspired discovery; two hosts in distinct /24 subnets suffice against long-running remote victims; discusses countermeasures. Adversary: remote attacker with two hosts, no prior position, patient (long-running victim).
bitmessage_link: Discovery-layer eclipse that bypasses connection-level hardening; relevant to peer-exchange in flooding messengers.

title: Eclipse Attacks on Ethereum's Peer-to-Peer Network
note: End-to-end eclipse of post-Merge Ethereum execution-layer nodes on restart: poisoning the discovery table, poisoning the DNS-based peer list via the official DNS crawler (28 IP addresses over 100 days) and hijacking idle incoming connection slots (outgoing redirection success from 45 to 95 percent). Adversary: remote attacker with a small set of IP addresses and patience, no network position.
bitmessage_link: Up-to-date check that overlay-eclipse remains practical, relevant for a modern flooding messenger.

title: Hijacking Bitcoin: Routing Attacks on Cryptocurrencies
note: Network-level routing attacks (BGP prefix hijacks, on-path interception) that partition Bitcoin or delay blocks; fewer than 100 prefixes isolate about half the mining power. Adversary: AS-level attacker with BGP control, or on-path observer.
bitmessage_link: Flood reachability depends on the Internet routing layer; a BGP-capable adversary can partition the flood and learn who connects to whom.

title: A Stealthier Partitioning Attack against Bitcoin Peer-to-Peer Network (Erebus)
note: Erebus: an AS-level attacker steers a victim's connections to attacker-controlled peers without BGP hijack by exploiting Bitcoin peer selection and network location of reachable nodes. Adversary: autonomous system that sits on many paths and can hold many addresses inside its prefixes.
bitmessage_link: Shows that peer-selection diversity rules are defeated by an AS-level adversary, a limit for IP-diversity hardening in flooding overlays.

title: TxProbe: Discovering Bitcoin's Network Topology Using Orphan Transactions
note: Reconstructs the Bitcoin network topology with precision and recall above 90 percent on testnet using orphan transactions. Adversary: active measurement node injecting crafted transactions; topology knowledge helps targeted eclipse and deanonymisation.
bitmessage_link: Topology hidden by design can be recovered by probing; flooding networks that rely on topology obscurity for privacy lose it.

title: Timing Analysis for Inferring the Topology of the Bitcoin Peer-to-Peer Network
note: Infers which peers are connected from block and transaction relay timing observed by a well-connected node. Adversary: passive observer with many connections measuring relay delays.
bitmessage_link: Timing leakage of a flooding network reveals overlay structure and neighbours of a source.

title: Measuring Ethereum Network Peers
note: Active crawling and passive measurement of the Ethereum P2P network (node churn, geography, client diversity, connectivity). Adversary: measurement crawler that can enumerate nodes through discovery.
bitmessage_link: Shows how easily a crawler enumerates a P2P overlay, the starting step for eclipse and deanonymisation.

title: GossipSub: Attack-Resilient Message Propagation in the Filecoin and ETH2.0 Networks
note: GossipSub v1.1: pub/sub routing with a local peer-scoring function, flood publishing, backoff, opportunistic grafting and peer-exchange hardening against Sybil, eclipse, censorship, cold-boot and covert-flash attacks. Adversary: Sybil nodes controlling a large fraction of the overlay that behave honestly in some phases (eclipse, censorship, spam, covert flash).
bitmessage_link: Pub/sub gossip with in-protocol resistance to Sybil and eclipse nodes; peer scoring is the opposite of Bitmessage's uniform trust in every peer.

title: GossipSub v1.1 specification
note: Normative specification of the v1.1 score function, mesh maintenance, flood publishing, prune backoff and peer exchange. Adversary: as in the GossipSub paper (Sybil and eclipse attackers, spammers, censors).
bitmessage_link: The deployed hardening of a gossip pub/sub layer, directly comparable to Bitmessage's unscored flood.

title: BASALT: A Rock-Solid Foundation for Epidemic Consensus Algorithms in Very Large, Very Open Networks
note: BASALT: Byzantine-tolerant random peer sampling that keeps close to optimal tolerance with a hit-counter and view-reset, using hash-based sampling without proof of stake. Adversary: permissionless setting where Byzantine nodes can flood the network with attacker identities up to a stated fraction.
bitmessage_link: A hardened membership layer that a flooding messenger could use in place of uniform peer lists to resist Sybil capture.

title: Total Eclipse of the Heart - Disrupting the InterPlanetary File System
note: Eclipse attacks on IPFS nodes and content using a Kademlia/libp2p peer-table weakness, with low resource use. Adversary: attacker able to create many peer IDs close to the victim in key space, with limited bandwidth.
bitmessage_link: Kademlia peer tables are eclipsed with cheap IDs; any DHT discovery used by a flooding messenger inherits this.

title: The Sybil Attack
note: Without a logically central identity authority, an entity can present multiple identities and defeat redundancy-based schemes. Adversary: single entity with many pseudonymous identities, limited only by resources.
bitmessage_link: Why per-identity trust fails in an open flooding network and why Bitmessage ties cost to objects (proof of work) instead of identities.

title: SoK: The Evolution of Sybil Defense via Social Networks
note: Systematises social-graph Sybil defences (SybilGuard to SybilRank) and their shared assumptions (fast mixing, attack edges). Adversary: Sybil attacker with limited attack edges into the honest region.
bitmessage_link: Shows the assumptions behind trust-graph admission control, which pseudonymous messengers with no social graph cannot make.

title: Aiding the Detection of Fake Accounts in Large Scale Social Online Services
note: SybilRank ranks accounts by early-terminated random-walk trust from known honest seeds to flag fake accounts at scale. Adversary: Sybil attacker with a bounded number of attack edges into the honest region.
bitmessage_link: Reputation-based admission control from a social graph; contrast with Bitmessage cost-based admission.

title: Identifying and characterizing Sybils in the Tor network
note: sybilhunter detects Sybil Tor relays from configuration similarity and uptime sequences; applied to nine years of archived consensus data, finds botnets, academic research relays and relays hijacking Bitcoin transactions; shows existing Sybil defences do not apply to Tor. Adversary: operator of many relays under multiple identities, using exit or HSDir positions.
bitmessage_link: Sybil operators in a volunteer overlay; relevant to peer-quality assumptions when using Tor as transport.

title: Spoiled Onions: Exposing Malicious Tor Exit Relays
note: Exitmap/probe study that finds malicious Tor exit relays performing MITM on traffic. Adversary: exit operator tampering with unencrypted or poorly protected application traffic.
bitmessage_link: Transport-level tampering by relays; end-to-end authentication of objects (as Bitmessage does) is needed on top of any anonymity network.

title: Users Get Routed: Traffic Correlation on Tor by Realistic Adversaries
note: Models Tor users and adversaries (relays, ASes, IXPs) and measures time-to-compromise with a Tor path simulator; users are far more exposed than earlier work estimated. Adversary: AS-level and IXP-level network adversaries and malicious relays, observing both ends over time.
bitmessage_link: Quantifies end-to-end correlation when Bitmessage is run through Tor; guard rotation and AS diversity matter.

title: RAPTOR: Routing Attacks on Privacy in Tor
note: Raptor attacks: asymmetric traffic analysis, BGP churn and prefix hijack/interception that let AS-level adversaries deanonymise Tor users; proposes monitoring defences. Adversary: AS-level adversary able to observe one direction of traffic at both ends and to announce BGP routes.
bitmessage_link: Network-position adversary against any Tor-based flooding client; global observation is feasible with BGP.

title: Measuring and mitigating AS-level adversaries against Tor
note: Measures how often AS-level adversaries sit on both ends of Tor circuits and proposes AS-aware path selection (Astoria). Adversary: single AS or colluding ASes on forward and reverse paths.
bitmessage_link: AS-aware path selection as a defence when relying on Tor for sender anonymity.

title: DeepCorr: Strong Flow Correlation Attacks on Tor Using Deep Learning
note: Deep-learning flow correlation correlates ingress and egress Tor flows far more accurately than statistical methods, with lower false-positive rates. Adversary: passive observer at both ends of a Tor circuit with only packet timing and size.
bitmessage_link: Tor does not defeat end-to-end correlation by a passive observer at both ends; a flood-and-trial-decrypt design must rely on cover traffic rather than the transport.

title: Trawling for Tor Hidden Services: Detection, Measurement, Deanonymization
note: Shows how an attacker can measure popularity of, take down, and deanonymise Tor hidden services by controlling HSDir positions and guards; evaluated on Silk Road and a botnet. Adversary: relay operator placing HSDirs near a descriptor and controlling the guard of the service.
bitmessage_link: Recipient privacy through hidden services is attackable via directory position and guard; why v3 onion services and vanguards were needed.

title: Circuit Fingerprinting Attacks: Passive Deanonymization of Tor Hidden Services
note: Identifies Tor hidden-service circuits and their traffic with a passive classifier on the client side (guard-level), then fingerprints hidden-service websites. Adversary: passive observer between the client and its guard.
bitmessage_link: Passive adversary at the user guard link can tell onion-service circuits; relevant when onion services carry Bitmessage-style traffic.

title: How Unique is Your .onion? An Analysis of the Fingerprintability of Tor Onion Services
note: Measures fingerprintability of onion services: some sites are easy to classify and a small set of features causes most errors. Adversary: local passive observer (network or guard) with training traces.
bitmessage_link: Which onion services leak under traffic analysis; informs sizing and padding of messenger traffic.

title: Effective Attacks and Provable Defenses for Website Fingerprinting
note: k-NN website fingerprinting attack and the Tamaraw-style provable defence analysis with overhead. Adversary: passive local observer, closed world and open world.
bitmessage_link: Padding cost versus fingerprinting; analogous cover-traffic tradeoffs for a messenger.

title: k-fingerprinting: a Robust Scalable Website Fingerprinting Technique
note: Random-forest based fingerprinting with fingerprint matching by k nearest neighbours, strong in open world and on hidden services. Adversary: passive local observer.
bitmessage_link: Stronger attacks reduce the safety margin of padding schemes.

title: Deep Fingerprinting: Undermining Website Fingerprinting Defenses with Deep Learning
note: Deep CNN fingerprinting reaches above 98 percent accuracy against undefended Tor and defeats WTF-PAD; partly defeats Walkie-Talkie. Adversary: passive local observer with large training set.
bitmessage_link: Light-weight padding defences are broken by deep learning; guidance for cover traffic in messengers.

title: Toward an Efficient Website Fingerprinting Defense
note: WTF-PAD adaptive padding fills gaps in the traffic timing distribution; no latency cost, moderate bandwidth. Adversary: passive local observer using state-of-the-art classifiers.
bitmessage_link: Adaptive padding as a transport-layer cover-traffic mechanism.

title: Walkie-Talkie: An Efficient Defense Against Passive Website Fingerprinting Attacks
note: Half-duplex burst molding defence with 31 percent bandwidth and 34 percent time overhead. Adversary: passive local observer with full website knowledge.
bitmessage_link: A concrete padding defence with measured overhead for a Tor-based transport.

title: Website Fingerprinting at Internet Scale
note: Shows fingerprinting scales to a large open world and identifies conditions under which classifiers remain effective. Adversary: passive local observer with limited training.
bitmessage_link: Realistic open-world numbers for traffic analysis.

title: An Empirical Study of the I2P Anonymity Network and its Censorship Resistance
note: Empirical measurement of I2P network size, churn, and censorship resistance with a block-list approach; shows I2P addresses can be enumerated. Adversary: censor or measurement operator that runs many I2P routers and crawls the netDb.
bitmessage_link: I2P as an alternative transport; the netDb is enumerable so peer-selection obscurity does not hold.

title: Practical Attacks against the I2P Network
note: Demonstrates practical attacks on I2P (Sybil router placement, tunnel selection, eepsite deanonymisation by timing). Adversary: attacker running a modest number of I2P routers who can influence peer selection and observe tunnel use.
bitmessage_link: Garlic-routing transport weaknesses in peer selection and tunnel construction.

title: Monitoring the I2P network
note: Monitoring infrastructure and measurement of I2P (peer discovery, popularity). Adversary: passive measurement operator with many routers.
bitmessage_link: Passive measurement of an anonymity network that a messenger could use as transport.

title: Can't you hear me knocking: Identification of user actions on Android apps via traffic analysis
note: Identifies user actions inside Android apps (including messaging apps) from encrypted traffic with high accuracy using SVM-style classifiers. Adversary: passive network observer (Wi-Fi sniffer or ISP) with no device access.
bitmessage_link: Even end-to-end encrypted messaging traffic leaks action types; flooding to everyone constant-rate mitigates this at bandwidth cost.

title: Careless Whisper: Exploiting Silent Delivery Receipts to Monitor Users on Mobile Instant Messengers
note: Silent delivery receipts let any user ping another without notice, inferring schedule, companion devices and OS, and exhausting battery or data. Adversary: any registered user knowing only a phone number, using crafted messages at high frequency.
bitmessage_link: Receipt metadata as a presence oracle; broadcast without recipient acknowledgement (Bitmessage) avoids this particular channel.

title: Improving Signal's Sealed Sender
note: Shows Signal's sealed sender leaks the sender via conversation timing and proposes fixes. Adversary: network-level observer or the Signal server correlating the delivery-receipt and reply timing.
bitmessage_link: Sender hiding by server blindness fails against timing; Bitmessage's broadcast avoids a server but gives up recipient privacy cost.

title: Tor proposal 247: Defending Against Guard Discovery Attacks using Vanguards
note: Proposal adding layered, long-lived second- and third-layer guards for onion-service circuits to defeat guard discovery. Adversary: relay operator that forces the service or client to build circuits repeatedly until an adversary relay lands next to the guard.
bitmessage_link: Defence against repeated circuit forcing; analogous to a flooding node being made to emit messages repeatedly.

title: Tor proposal 292: Mesh-based vanguards
note: Revises vanguards to a mesh of second- and third-layer guards with rotation periods, the version deployed in Tor. Adversary: as for proposal 247 (guard discovery by circuit forcing).
bitmessage_link: Deployed layered-guard construction to protect long-running onion services.

title: Tor proposal 333: Vanguards lite
note: Lightweight vanguards enabled by default for all clients: one extra layer of guard for non-onion circuits. Adversary: guard-discovery attacker with limited resources.
bitmessage_link: Default-on version of the guard-discovery defence.

title: Tor Vanguards Specification
note: Current normative text of vanguards motivation and parameters. Adversary: guard-discovery attacker; compromised guard through coercion or Netflow purchase.
bitmessage_link: Reference description of Tor vanguards.

title: Tor proposal 327: A First Take at PoW Over Introduction Circuits
note: Client puzzles (Equi-X, later) attached to onion-service introduction requests with a service-set effort level so that a flooding adversary pays CPU per request. Adversary: remote attacker who floods introduction points to exhaust a service (resource DoS), cannot be detected by identity.
bitmessage_link: Production proof-of-work admission control with a dynamic effort target, the successor to the fixed per-object proof of work in Bitmessage.

title: Tor proposal 224: Next-Generation Hidden Services in Tor
note: Design of v3 onion services: ed25519 keys, blinded keys per time period for HSDir descriptor privacy, client authorisation. Adversary: HSDir operators and relay-level adversaries enumerating or tracking onion services; addresses the weaknesses in v2 (Trawling).
bitmessage_link: Descriptor blinding to stop directory enumeration; relevant to private recipient rendezvous.

title: Hashcash - A Denial of Service Counter-Measure
note: Partial-hash-collision stamps as a cost-function against email spam and DoS. Adversary: bulk sender who trades CPU for volume; assumes a roughly uniform sender cost model.
bitmessage_link: The exact mechanism Bitmessage attaches to every object.

title: Proof-of-Work Proves Not to Work
note: Argues that PoW cannot separate spammers from legitimate senders because spammers use stolen cycles (zombies) while honest users have weak machines; a cost that spammers will pay is too high for ordinary users. Adversary: botnet-equipped spammer with free compute.
bitmessage_link: The standard economic argument against Bitmessage-style flat proof of work: the cost falls on honest low-power senders, not on botnets.

title: Proof of Work can Work
note: Rebuts Laurie and Clayton: with sender-specific, reputation-adjusted difficulty, PoW can impose cost on spammers while sparing trusted senders. Adversary: spammer who must pay marginal cost per message; recommended difficulty tied to reputation.
bitmessage_link: Suggests per-sender difficulty tied to reputation; Bitmessage has no reputation so cannot use it.

title: The Economics of Spam
note: Economic analysis of spam: costs imposed on users versus spammer profit, conversion rates, and where interventions bite. Adversary: profit-seeking spammer with tiny conversion rates.
bitmessage_link: Gives the economic frame for setting a per-message proof-of-work target.

title: Equihash: Asymmetric Proof-of-Work Based on the Generalized Birthday Problem
note: Memory-hard, asymmetric PoW (cheap verification) designed to narrow the ASIC advantage. Adversary: attacker with specialised hardware (ASIC/FPGA) and time-memory trade-offs.
bitmessage_link: Memory-hard PoW narrows the CPU/GPU/ASIC gap that makes flat PoW favour attackers.

title: Argon2: the memory-hard function for password hashing and other applications
venue: Argon2 specification v1.3 (companion paper at IEEE EuroS&P 2016)
note: Memory-hard function family with tunable memory, time and parallelism; used as the basis of memory-hard PoW and client puzzles. Adversary: GPU/ASIC cracker or time-memory tradeoff attacker.
bitmessage_link: Candidate building block for memory-hard per-object stamps.

title: Scrypt is Maximally Memory-Hard
note: Proves scrypt has maximal cumulative memory complexity in the parallel random oracle model, justifying memory-hard PoW. Adversary: parallel attacker with unlimited cores and bounded memory.
bitmessage_link: Formal justification for memory-hard stamps.

title: Proofs of Space
note: Proof-of-space protocols where the prover must prove it dedicates disk space; proposed as alternative to PoW for spam control and mining. Adversary: prover with limited storage and fast recomputation.
bitmessage_link: Replaces CPU burn with storage commitment as the admission cost.

title: Proofs of Useful Work
note: Constructs proofs of work whose solution also solves worst-case-hard computational problems (OV, 3SUM, APSP). Adversary: prover with polynomial resources and fine-grained complexity assumptions.
bitmessage_link: Candidate for making stamps useful to someone, reducing waste.

title: Primecoin: Cryptocurrency with Prime Number Proof-of-Work
note: Chains of prime numbers as proof of work with scientific value. Adversary: miner with special hardware advantage.
bitmessage_link: Early useful-PoW example.

title: Balloon Hashing: A Memory-Hard Function Providing Provable Protection Against Sequential Attacks
note: Memory-hard function with proven space-time lower bounds against sequential attackers. Adversary: sequential attacker with space-time trade-offs.
bitmessage_link: Alternative memory-hard primitive for stamps.

title: Nostr NIP-13: Proof of Work
note: Optional hashcash-style leading-zero-bit commitment on event IDs, usable by relays as an anti-spam filter. Adversary: spammer posting events to relays.
bitmessage_link: Direct descendant of Bitmessage-style per-object proof of work in a relay-based system, optional rather than mandatory.

title: EIP-627: Whisper Specification
note: Whisper v6 specification: topic-based gossip messaging with per-message proof of work, TTL, Bloom-filter topic subscriptions to cut bandwidth. Adversary: spammers and network observers; PoW bounds spam and Bloom filters leak interest of subscribers.
bitmessage_link: Direct Bitmessage-like gossip messenger with per-message PoW; its failure to scale spam resistance motivated Waku RLN.

title: Privacy Pass: Bypassing Internet Challenges Anonymously
note: VOPRF-based tokens: issue after one challenge, redeem later unlinkably to skip CAPTCHAs; includes batched DLEQ proofs. Adversary: malicious issuer or colluding issuer and edge that try to link redemption to issuance; attacker who tries to double-spend tokens.
bitmessage_link: Anonymous, unlinkable admission tokens for rate-limited access; a way to replace per-message proof of work with issued tokens.

title: RFC 9576: The Privacy Pass Architecture
note: Architecture of Privacy Pass with Client, Attester, Issuer and Origin and deployment models (same-party and split) and privacy considerations (issuer view, collusion, token-count side channels). Adversary: colluding issuer, attester and origin who link users through timing, token metadata or anonymity-set size.
bitmessage_link: Standard framework for admission tokens that carry no identity.

title: RFC 9577: The Privacy Pass HTTP Authentication Scheme
note: HTTP authentication scheme and token challenge format for Privacy Pass. Adversary: origin that tries to link tokens across redemptions via challenge reuse or per-origin binding.
bitmessage_link: Wire format for anonymous tokens; applicable to relay admission.

title: RFC 9578: Privacy Pass Issuance Protocols
note: Two issuance protocols: privately verifiable (VOPRF) and publicly verifiable (blind RSA). Adversary: malicious issuer attempting key-based tagging attacks; attacker replaying tokens.
bitmessage_link: Concrete token types for stamps.

title: RFC 9497: Oblivious Pseudorandom Functions (OPRFs) Using Prime-Order Groups
note: OPRF, VOPRF and POPRF over prime-order groups; building block for Privacy Pass and PSI. Adversary: malicious client or server, with verifiability to detect a key-switching server.
bitmessage_link: Primitive behind unlinkable tokens.

title: RFC 9474: RSA Blind Signatures
note: RSABSSA blind signature scheme (RSA-PSS) with public verifiability. Adversary: malicious signer attempting to link signatures to signing sessions, and forger attempting one-more forgery.
bitmessage_link: Token type for publicly verifiable anonymous admission.

title: Algebraic MACs and Keyed-Verification Anonymous Credentials
note: Algebraic MACs from which keyed-verification anonymous credentials (issuer = verifier) are built, cheaper than pairing-based credentials. Adversary: malicious users trying to forge or share credentials, and verifier trying to link presentations.
bitmessage_link: Efficient anonymous credentials for a single operator or relay that both issues and verifies.

title: The Signal Private Group System and Anonymous Credentials Supporting Efficient Verifiable Encryption
note: KVAC-based group membership credentials so the server enforces membership without learning the member list. Adversary: honest-but-curious server and non-member attackers.
bitmessage_link: Server-enforced admission without a membership list; relevant to chans and group membership.

title: Anonymous Tokens with Private Metadata Bit
note: Anonymous tokens with a private metadata bit (e.g., a spam score) that only the issuer can read. Adversary: user wanting to read or change the metadata bit; issuer wanting to link.
bitmessage_link: Tokens that carry a reputation bit without identity.

title: WAKU-RLN-RELAY: Privacy-Preserving Peer-to-Peer Economic Spam Protection
note: Relay-layer spam protection for gossip routing using rate-limiting nullifiers: each peer proves in zero knowledge that its identity is in a membership Merkle tree and it has not exceeded its epoch rate, and double-signalling reveals the secret key via Shamir shares for slashing. Adversary: spammer with arbitrarily many messages or identities who has to stake for each identity, and non-member Sybils; not designed against network-level adversaries.
bitmessage_link: Replaces per-message proof of work with a staked rate limit, solving the honest-user cost and botnet asymmetry problems of Bitmessage PoW.

title: Waku: A Family of Modular P2P Protocols For Secure & Censorship-Resistant Communication
note: Describes Waku, a family of modular P2P messaging protocols (relay, store, filter, light push) built on libp2p gossipsub with RLN spam protection and ephemeral messaging. Adversary: censoring peers and spammers; no strong network-level adversary.
bitmessage_link: Modern successor of Whisper and spiritual neighbour of Bitmessage in a pub/sub messenger setting.

title: Message Latency in Waku Relay with Rate Limiting Nullifiers
note: Simulations and measurements of gossip latency in Waku relay with RLN proof generation and verification overhead. Adversary: none (performance), uses spam-rate workloads.
bitmessage_link: Cost side of replacing PoW with zero-knowledge rate limits (proving time on mobile).

title: 32/RLN-V1: Rate Limit Nullifier
note: Specification of RLN v1: Groth16 circuit proving Merkle membership and a Shamir share of the secret, with internal nullifier to detect duplicate signalling in an epoch. Adversary: spammer sending more than one message per epoch (breaks to reveal secret), and registration Sybil attacker (cost of registration is the bound).
bitmessage_link: The rate-limiting primitive for message admission without identity.

title: RLN-V2: Rate Limit Nullifier v2
note: RLN v2 allows a per-user message limit greater than one per epoch by using a message id range and a polynomial of higher degree. Adversary: as for v1; user exceeding its allocated limit.
bitmessage_link: Flexible per-user rate limits; closer to a stamp budget.

title: 17/WAKU2-RLN-RELAY
note: Normative spec integrating RLN into Waku relay: membership contract, epoch length, proof validation before forwarding, slashing and spam handling. Adversary: spammers inside membership and gossip peers that relay invalid proofs.
bitmessage_link: How a deployed gossip messenger validates admission proofs before relaying.

title: WAKU-MIX
note: Libp2p-based mixnet integration for Waku (sphinx packets, per-hop delays) giving sender anonymity for publish and request-response. Adversary: global passive observer limited by delay mixing, with some malicious mix nodes.
bitmessage_link: A mixnet layer in front of a gossip pub/sub, the post-Bitmessage design point for sender anonymity.

title: Mix DoS Protection
note: Design for protecting mix nodes from flooding by senders: per-packet proofs and rate limits at the first hop. Adversary: spammer or Sybil sender that floods mix nodes with packets.
bitmessage_link: Admission control for mix traffic, the mixnet equivalent of Bitmessage proof of work.

title: RLN DoS Protection for Mixnet
note: Mix DoS protection using RLN proofs per Sphinx packet. Adversary: sender exceeding its per-epoch message allowance or replaying proofs across mix nodes.
bitmessage_link: Zero-knowledge rate limit as mixnet admission.

title: Multi-message_id Burn RLN
note: RLN variant where a user can burn several message ids in one proof to send a burst. Adversary: spammer reusing message ids.
bitmessage_link: Burst budget for rate limiting.

title: Message Franking via Committing Authenticated Encryption
note: Formalises message franking for abuse reporting in end-to-end encrypted messaging: the recipient can prove to the platform what the sender sent, without the platform reading messages. Adversary: malicious sender who tries to send content the recipient cannot report, or malicious recipient who fabricates reports.
bitmessage_link: Abuse and spam accountability in an end-to-end encrypted system; Bitmessage has no reporting path at all.

title: Asymmetric Message Franking: Content Moderation for Metadata-Private End-to-End Encryption
note: Message franking that works with sender-anonymous (sealed-sender style) delivery so platforms can moderate reported content without learning the sender at send time. Adversary: abusive sender hidden from the platform, and malicious reporter who forges reports.
bitmessage_link: Spam and abuse moderation compatible with sender-anonymous delivery.

title: A Critical Evaluation of Website Fingerprinting Attacks
note: Shows laboratory website-fingerprinting results depend on strong assumptions (browser version, time gap, tabbed browsing, background traffic) that weaken in realistic settings. Adversary: passive local observer whose training data may differ from the victim environment.
bitmessage_link: Cautions that traffic-analysis results are assumption-sensitive; relevant when deciding how much cover traffic a messenger needs.

title: The Sniper Attack: Anonymously Deanonymizing and Disabling the Tor Network
note: A single client can exhaust relay memory with unread SENDME-driven cells, taking down targeted relays and thereby forcing circuits through attacker-controlled relays. Adversary: low-bandwidth client that can open circuits and withhold reads; anonymity of the attacker preserved.
bitmessage_link: Flow-control DoS in the anonymity transport; denial of service as a deanonymisation primitive.

title: All the Numbers are US: Large-scale Abuse of Contact Discovery in Mobile Messengers
note: Crawls of WhatsApp, Signal and Telegram contact discovery enumerate registered phone numbers at scale and reverse hash-based discovery protocols. Adversary: any client who can query the contact-discovery service at high rate with a database of mobile numbers; no server compromise.
bitmessage_link: Registration and lookup oracles are the usual spam and enumeration surface of identity-based messengers; Bitmessage avoids phone numbers but pays with address-free flooding.

title: Counter-RAPTOR: Safeguarding Tor Against Active Routing Attacks
note: Defences against BGP prefix hijack/interception of Tor guards: resilience-aware guard selection and monitoring. Adversary: AS-level active attacker announcing malicious routes to capture guard traffic.
bitmessage_link: Peer (guard) selection hardened against routing adversaries.

title: Var-CNN: A Data-Efficient Website Fingerprinting Attack Based on Deep Learning
note: Variable-input CNN fingerprinting that works with small training sets and combines timing and direction. Adversary: passive local observer with limited training data.
bitmessage_link: Fingerprinting works with little training data; messenger padding must assume it.

title: Automated Website Fingerprinting through Deep Learning
note: Deep learning removes manual feature engineering for website fingerprinting; evaluated closed world and open world on Tor. Adversary: passive local observer.
bitmessage_link: Traffic analysis as a trained classifier; no handcrafted features needed.

title: Tik-Tok: The Utility of Packet Timing in Website Fingerprinting Attacks
note: Shows packet timing, in addition to direction, strongly improves website fingerprinting against Tor and defeats several padding defences. Adversary: passive local observer who records inter-packet times.
bitmessage_link: Timing is the leak that padding must hide; a flooding messenger sending at fixed cadence removes this feature.

title: Online Website Fingerprinting: Evaluating Website Fingerprinting Attacks on Tor in the Real World
note: Evaluates fingerprinting on the live Tor network with a mix of user-like conditions and finds real-world accuracy lower than laboratory results but still meaningful. Adversary: passive local observer in the wild (no lab control).
bitmessage_link: Calibrates how much real-world traffic analysis threat remains for onion-service based messengers.

title: Zero-delay Lightweight Defenses against Website Fingerprinting
note: FRONT and GLUE: padding defences that add no delay and little overhead by front-loading dummy packets. Adversary: passive local observer with adaptive attacker.
bitmessage_link: Cheap cover traffic designs for the transport layer.

title: Content and popularity analysis of Tor hidden services
note: Harvested hidden service descriptors (via HSDir position) to enumerate services and estimate popularity and content. Adversary: operator of HSDir relays sampling descriptors.
bitmessage_link: Onion address enumeration through directory position; relevant to onion-service addressing for private chat.

title: Coconut: Threshold Issuance Selective Disclosure Credentials with Applications to Distributed Ledgers
note: Threshold, blind issuance of re-randomisable selective-disclosure credentials by a set of authorities, unlinkable use; basis of Nym credentials. Adversary: fewer than threshold malicious authorities; users trying to forge or share; verifiers trying to link.
bitmessage_link: Decentralised issuer set for anonymous admission tokens (no single issuer to trust).

title: Changing of the Guards: A Framework for Understanding and Improving Entry Guard Selection in Tor
note: Framework for entry guard parameters (number, lifetime) trading profiling resistance against availability; recommends fewer guards with longer lifetimes. Adversary: relay adversary controlling a fraction of bandwidth who is selected as a guard for some users over time.
bitmessage_link: Peer-selection hardening for the user side of an anonymity network.

title: Safely Measuring Tor
note: PrivCount: secure multi-party counting with differential privacy so relays can publish usage statistics safely. Adversary: compromised relays and statistics collectors seeking per-user data.
bitmessage_link: Method to measure onion service usage without harming users.

title: Peek-a-Boo, I Still See You: Why Efficient Traffic Analysis Countermeasures Fail
note: Shows coarse features (bandwidth, duration, bursts) defeat popular low-overhead padding countermeasures across several classifiers. Adversary: passive observer with a labelled training set and chosen classifiers.
bitmessage_link: Bounds what cheap padding achieves; supports preferring full cover traffic or flooding to padding.

title: Revisiting BBS Signatures
note: Security proof of BBS signatures in the algebraic group model with a tighter reduction; BBS underlies selective-disclosure anonymous credentials. Adversary: forger with chosen-message access in AGM.
bitmessage_link: Signature primitive for multi-show unlinkable credentials.

title: zk-promises: Anonymous Moderation, Reputation, and Blocking from Anonymous Credentials with Callbacks
note: Anonymous credentials with callbacks: a server can later ban, penalise or update reputation of an anonymous user without learning who they are. Adversary: misbehaving anonymous user who tries to evade moderation, and server trying to link sessions.
bitmessage_link: Anonymous reputation and revocation, the missing counterpart to Bitmessage's unaccountable senders.

title: BLACR: TTP-Free Blacklistable Anonymous Credentials with Reputation
note: Anonymous blacklisting with reputation scores and no trusted third party; users prove their score is acceptable without revealing identity. Adversary: misbehaving anonymous user and a server that wants to link sessions; no TTP for revocation.
bitmessage_link: Reputation-based admission for anonymous senders, as an alternative to per-object proof of work.

title: Anon-Pass: Practical Anonymous Subscriptions
note: Anonymous subscription credentials with a limit on access frequency (epoch-based token) and linkability within an epoch to deter sharing. Adversary: malicious subscriber sharing credentials, honest-but-curious service provider.
bitmessage_link: A deployed-in-concept rate-limited anonymous credential, close to RLN in intent.

title: Decentralized Lightweight Detection of Eclipse Attacks on Bitcoin Clients
note: Lightweight client-side eclipse detection using a gossiped block-header check against a small set of independent peers. Adversary: eclipse attacker controlling all or most of the victim connections.
bitmessage_link: Detection layer for eclipsed flooding nodes (compare views with out-of-band witnesses).

title: Perigee: Efficient Peer-to-Peer Network Design for Blockchains
note: Adaptive peer selection: nodes rank neighbours by first-delivery time and replace the slowest, producing low-latency topologies. Adversary: none considered, but selection by delivery time is exploitable by strategic peers.
bitmessage_link: Peer selection driven by delivery time conflicts with source anonymity (early deliverers are rewarded).

title: On the Limits of Provable Anonymity
note: Shows that strong provable anonymity against a powerful network adversary requires unrealistic assumptions on traffic or cover. Adversary: global passive adversary able to compromise some nodes.
bitmessage_link: Cited limit result for flooding schemes that claim anonymity without cover traffic.

title: Honey Onions: a Framework for Characterizing and Identifying Misbehaving Tor HSDirs
note: Honey onions: decoy onion services detect HSDir relays that snoop on descriptors; at least 110 snooping HSDirs over 72 days, more than half on cloud infrastructure and delaying use of learned data. Adversary: malicious HSDir operators harvesting onion addresses and probing the services.
bitmessage_link: Detects misbehaving directory nodes that enumerate rendezvous addresses; relevant to private rendezvous points for messaging.

title: The Cost of Stability: Deanonymizing Onion Services Long-Lived Introduction Circuits
note: Intersection attack that exploits onion-service introduction circuits fixed for 18-24 hours: an adaptive adversary observing one relay at a time reconstructs the full circuit and locates the service; on live Tor, nine of nine runs succeeded with median time about 2.2 hours. Adversary: adaptive observer of one Tor relay at a time (a compromised or malicious relay), no global view.
bitmessage_link: Persistent circuit state in onion services as a deanonymisation surface for long-running receivers.

title: Time will Tell: Large-scale De-anonymization of Hidden I2P Services via Live Behavior Alignment (Extended Version)
note: I2PERCEPTION: low-cost method that reveals IP addresses of I2P hidden services by deploying floodfill routers to passively collect RouterInfo and aligning publication behaviour with live service behaviour. Adversary: attacker running floodfill routers (no need to control tunnel participants), passive.
bitmessage_link: Recent I2P attack showing behavioural correlation defeats garlic routing.

title: Examining I2P Resilience: Effect of Centrality-based Attack
note: Models I2P as a graph and evaluates removal of high-centrality routers. Adversary: attacker capable of removing or degrading the most central routers.
bitmessage_link: Availability limits of an anonymity network transport.

title: Anonymous Rate-Limited Credentials (draft-yun-cfrg-arc-01)
note: Keyed-verification anonymous credential that can be presented up to a fixed number of times per context, each presentation bound to client secrets and public application context and unlinkable to other presentations. Adversary: client trying to exceed its presentation limit or link/forge; issuer-verifier trying to link presentations.
bitmessage_link: Standards-track form of the anonymous rate limit that RLN provides on-chain; direct replacement for per-object proof of work.

title: Anonymous Credit Tokens (draft-schlesinger-cfrg-act-01)
note: Anonymous credit tokens carrying a spendable balance: the client spends part of the credit per request and receives change, with unlinkable presentation and double-spend prevention. Adversary: client trying to double-spend or overspend; issuer trying to link spends.
bitmessage_link: Budgeted anonymous admission (credits per request) as a generalisation of one-token-per-message stamps.

title: The BBS Signature Scheme (draft-irtf-cfrg-bbs-signatures-12)
note: Specification of BBS signatures with multi-message signing and unlinkable zero-knowledge proofs of knowledge supporting selective disclosure. Adversary: forger under q-type assumption in pairing groups; verifier attempting to link proofs.
bitmessage_link: Primitive for unlinkable multi-show credentials, e.g. membership or reputation proofs without identity.

title: Eclipse Attacks on Monero's Peer-to-Peer Network
note: First practical eclipse of Monero: classic eclipse attacks fail against its connection manager, so the attacker forces the target to reset benign connections and reconnect to malicious nodes (no restart needed); countermeasures reported to the Monero team. Adversary: remote attacker with several malicious nodes that exploits connection-management rules; relevant because Dandelion++ privacy relies on honest outbound peers.
bitmessage_link: An eclipsed node loses Dandelion-style source hiding and sees only attacker traffic; peer-selection hardening is a prerequisite for stem-phase privacy.

title: SybilControl: Practical Sybil Defense with Computational Puzzles
venue: ACM Workshop on Scalable Trusted Computing (STC) 2012
note: Sybil defence for decentralised systems in which every identity must keep solving periodic computational puzzles to remain valid, bounding identities per unit of compute. Adversary: Sybil attacker with finite compute (no ASIC/botnet assumption) and fixed lifetime of puzzle solutions.
bitmessage_link: Identity-level (not object-level) puzzle admission; contrasts with Bitmessage per-object PoW and shows the same botnet and hardware-asymmetry limits.

title: An Empirical Analysis of Privacy in the Lightning Network
note: Empirical analysis of privacy in the Lightning Network: heuristics linking channels and nodes to on-chain entities and inferring payment paths; shows route and endpoint information leaks. Adversary: passive observer of the public channel graph and blockchain, optionally with a few well-placed routing nodes.
bitmessage_link: Onion-routed payment paths as a Tor-like propagation substrate and its measured leakage.

title: One Bad Apple Spoils the Bunch: Transaction DoS in MimbleWimble Blockchains
note: New denial-of-service attack on MimbleWimble (Beam) combining Dandelion++ private relay with transaction aggregation: an adversary controlling 10 percent of nodes can stop over 45 percent of transactions from reaching the blockchain. Adversary: minority of nodes in the stem path that silently drop or corrupt aggregated transactions; mitigations discussed.
bitmessage_link: Source-hiding relay without validation opens a spam channel; the privacy-versus-abuse-control trade-off for any stem phase.

title: On the Inherent Anonymity of Gossiping
note: Differential-privacy (epsilon-DP) analysis of the source anonymity of gossip: any gossip protocol on a poorly connected graph cannot give meaningful anonymity (fundamental limit); on graphs with controlled connectivity, cobra walks give tangible guarantees, and the proof technique extends to Dandelion; the analysis exposes the trade-off between dissemination time and source anonymity. Adversary: observer of the dissemination (source-detection adversary) reasoning about which node started the gossip.
bitmessage_link: Theory result on source anonymity of epidemic dissemination, the setting Bitmessage and its Dandelion stem sit in.

title: Security Analysis of Bitcoin's V2 Transport Protocol: Exploiting Design Implications for Sustained Eclipse and Downgrade Attacks
note: Security analysis of Bitcoin V2 (BIP324) encrypted P2P transport: a network-level attacker can identify application messages from TCP payload lengths, eclipse a node via properties of encrypted channels, and downgrade all connections to the unencrypted protocol using the compatibility mechanisms; validated with measurements, emulation and simulation. Adversary: on-path network-level attacker (active for eclipse and downgrade).
bitmessage_link: Encrypted transport alone does not remove length leakage or downgrade risk for a flooding network; relevant to any messenger that layers transport encryption under flooding.

title: Early-MFC: Enhanced Flow Correlation Attacks on Tor via Multi-view Triplet Networks with Early Network Traffic
note: Early-MFC: flow correlation using only the early part of a connection via multi-view triplet networks over payload sizes and inter-packet delays. Adversary: passive observer of both ends of a Tor connection who must decide quickly from short traces.
bitmessage_link: Correlation needs only short traces, so short Tor sessions for a messenger are not safe.
